originalRecord.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Production first moves from F to C and then from C to D, with resources and technology unchanged. Why does only the second move clearly sacrifice Y for more X?
options: The first uses slack to raise both outputs; the second reallocates along the frontier
The first creates growth; growth eliminates opportunity cost on the second
F is unattainable, so its output cannot be compared with C
D lies inside the frontier and therefore wastes Y
originalRecord.feedback: F to C raises both outputs by improving use of existing capacity. C to D moves between efficient frontier points, gaining X at the expense of Y.

beforeRecord.q: Use the graph. Production moves from F to C and then from C to D, with resources and technology unchanged. Which output changes show the first move using idle capacity and the second involving a tradeoff?
options: F to C: gain 7 X and 15 Y; C to D: gain 6 X and give up 15 Y
F to C: gain 7 X and 10 Y; C to D: gain 6 X and give up 15 Y
F to C: gain 6 X and 15 Y; C to D: gain 7 X and give up 10 Y
F to C: gain 8 X and 10 Y; C to D: gain 6 X and give up 20 Y
beforeRecord.feedback: F=(8,20), C=(15,35), and D=(21,20). F to C adds 7 X and 15 Y by moving from inside the frontier to it. C to D adds 6 X at the cost of 15 Y along the frontier.

afterRecord.q: Production moves from F to C and then from C to D with resources and technology unchanged. Which explanation, supported by the graph’s output changes, explains why only the second move sacrifices Y for more X?
options: F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
afterRecord.feedback: F=(8,20) lies inside the PPF, while C=(15,35) and D=(21,20) lie on it. F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y without expanding capacity. C to D reallocates fully employed resources: gaining 6 X requires giving up 15 Y.

review.drift_problem: The revised stem labels the first move as using idle capacity and the second as a tradeoff. Every option has both outputs rising first and X rising at Y’s expense second; only arithmetic distinguishes them.
review.economic_and_graph_evidence: Read F=(8,20), C=(15,35), D=(21,20); identify F inside and C/D on the same frontier. The key combines these output differences with the appropriate resource-use explanation.

options: Binding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Binding floor: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding floor: $1,000 is above equilibrium.
originalRecord.feedback: A price ceiling is binding when it is set below the market equilibrium price. The graph places the ceiling at $1,000, below the $2,000 equilibrium rent.

afterRecord.q: A legal maximum rent of $1,000 is shown. Which classification and equilibrium reading are correct?
options: A binding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.

A nonbinding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
A binding floor; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
afterRecord.feedback: The demand and supply curves intersect at $2,000. The legal maximum of $1,000 is a price ceiling. It is below equilibrium, so it prevents the market from clearing at $2,000 and is binding.
